title: Sourdough Pancakes
subtitle: American-style thick pancakes risen with sourdough discard
excerpt: Thick, fluffy American-style pancakes with a gentle tang from sourdough discard. A good use for the starter you'd otherwise throw away, and considerably more interesting than a plain buttermilk stack.
sourceNotes: Sourdough discard pancakes have become a popular technique among home bakers who maintain a sourdough starter. This version balances the tang of the discard with baking powder and bicarbonate of soda for reliable lift.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cooked pancakes freeze well. Stack with baking paper between them, freeze flat, then reheat in a toaster or dry pan.
recipe.batchNotes: Double or triple the batch and freeze extras for weekday breakfasts.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Mix the dry and wet ingredients separately the night before. Combine and cook in the morning.

glossaryTerms.definition: The portion of sourdough starter removed before feeding; used in pancakes, waffles, and crackers for flavour and leavening without waste.

content.text: Sourdough pancakes take the standard American breakfast pancake and add a gentle, yoghurt-like tang, an open crumb, and a depth of flavour that plain baking-powder pancakes can't match. The key ingredient is the
discard

, the portion of starter removed before feeding. It gives both flavour and an acidity that works with the bicarbonate of soda to create lift. The result is thick, fluffy, and golden with crisp edges. The intermediate difficulty rating is there because reading batter consistency and pan heat takes practice. The method itself is straightforward.

items.prepNote: discard or fed starter, at room temperature

content.text: About the starter

Unfed {{sourdough-starter}} discard is ideal here. It is more acidic than fresh starter, which gives the pancakes more tang. That acidity also helps the bicarbonate of soda do its work; bicarbonate needs an acid to activate, and sourdough provides it without requiring buttermilk. Recently-fed starter works too. The pancakes will simply be a little milder and slightly less risen.
Making the batter

In a large bowl, combine the {{sourdough-starter}} starter, {{eggs}} eggs, {{whole-milk}} milk, and melted {{unsalted-butter}} butter. Whisk until smooth. In a separate bowl, mix the {{plain-flour}} flour, {{caster-sugar}} sugar, {{baking-powder}} baking powder, {{bicarbonate-of-soda}} bicarbonate of soda, and {{sea-salt-flakes}} salt. Tip the dry ingredients into the wet bowl and stir gently until just combined. Stop as soon as no dry flour remains, lumps are fine, and overmixing deflates the batter and makes the pancakes tough.

Leave the batter to sit for five minutes while the pan heats. You'll often see it puff slightly as the bicarbonate reacts with the sourdough's acidity. Don't be tempted to stir it again at this point.
Cooking the pancakes

Set a frying pan over medium heat. Add a small knob of butter and let it melt until it foams. Drop a heaped tablespoon of batter into the pan for a test pancake, if it spreads sluggishly and the edges look heavy, thin the batter with a splash of milk. The pancake should spread to about 8 to 9 cm naturally.

Cook for 2 to 3 minutes until bubbles appear across the surface and the edges look set and dry. Flip with a spatula and cook for a further 1 to 2 minutes until the underside is golden. The key is not to press down on the pancake after flipping, the trapped air inside is what makes the fluffy texture.
Keep finished pancakes warm in a low oven (around 100°C) while you cook the rest. Add a tiny piece of butter to the pan every few pancakes to maintain the right surface.
Serving

Stack and serve with {{maple-syrup}} maple syrup. Also good with sliced banana and a drizzle of honey, or with streaky bacon and butter if you want the full American diner treatment. The slight tang of the sourdough works particularly well against the sweetness of maple syrup.
Troubleshooter
Pancakes are flat and dense:
Check the baking powder and bicarbonate of soda are fresh, both lose potency quickly. Also check the starter isn't too old and acidic; very sour discard can over-acidify and kill the lift.
Outsides are browning before insides cook through:
The heat is too high. Reduce to medium-low. Sourdough pancakes are thicker than British-style and need more time at a gentler heat.
Batter seems too thick:
Different starters have different hydrations. Add milk a tablespoon at a time until the batter drops from the spoon in a thick ribbon rather than holding its shape.
